Reasoning

03 · argue, attack, survive, weigh

Why there is no mesh

the lenses cannot see each other, on purpose

Nine lenses read the same evidence and never each other's conclusions. There is no parameter through which one view could reach another — it is structural, not an instruction in a prompt. Lenses that see each other converge, converging rebuilds consensus, and consensus scores zero. The diversity is the asset being protected.

What agreement is worth

less than it looks

Agreement between lenses is not presented as corroboration anywhere in this system. Isolation prevents convergence in language; it does not prevent correlated error. They read overlapping documents, so five being wrong together is about as likely as one. The judge is told to weigh by materiality — six lenses agreeing on a weak signal lose to one carrying the company's own guidance with a quote.

mechanicalstated 0.5 → survived 0.25 · eroded 0.25
argued

This is a purely mechanical, non-judgmental extrapolation model, and its value lies precisely in that discipline: it takes a long history (20-28 reported periods), applies a shrunk median growth/level estimator (which dampens the influence of outlier quarters), and projects forward without narrative bias. For net sales, using Q1 FY2026 (41800/41765) as the anchor and applying a modest shrunk median growth rate to get ~41835 is a sensible, low-drama baseline — it correctly avoids extrapolating from a single quarter's swing and anchors to the most recent actual. The comparable sales figure similarly falls back to a long-run shrunk median (0.2) rather than chasing the most recent print (2.2), which guards against overfitting to one strong quarter. The strongest piece of evidence is the recency and consistency of the Q1 FY2026 net sales figures across two independent citations (41765 and 41800), which validates the anchor point for the sales projection.

attacked

The mechanical method breaks down badly in the EPS case: citing 'fiscal 2025: -3.6' alongside quarterly values of 2.72 and 3.43 signals a severe basis mismatch — that -3.6 figure is almost certainly a full-year GAAP or one-time-impaired diluted EPS (likely reflecting a large impairment/goodwill charge, e.g., SRS-related) being blended into a growth-rate calculation against adjusted quarterly EPS figures that are structurally incomparable in scale and basis (annual vs. quarterly, adjusted vs. reported, negative vs. positive). A median-based growth rate computed across a series containing full-year negative EPS and quarterly positive EPS is arithmetically incoherent and produces a result (4.33) that cannot be sanity-checked against the plain trend (2.72 → 3.43 already implies solid sequential/YoY growth without needing a distorted 'shrunk median'). Additionally, for net sales, Q4 is seasonally the weakest quarter and Q1 the strongest for home improvement retail — projecting forward from Q1's 41800 using a 'shrunk median growth rate' derived from a mixed-seasonality 26-period history risks smuggling in a seasonal step-change as if it were organic growth, since Q2 is typically HD's strongest sales quarter, meaning 41835 could be a significant underestimate if seasonality isn't explicitly modeled. The comparable-sales figure (0.2) is also suspect: it ignores that the trend has clearly been accelerating (0.4 → 0.6 → 2.2), and a 28-period historical median swamps this recent acceleration signal, meaning the model is anchored to stale multi-year history rather than the current trajectory the company itself is reporting. This is the classic 'extrapolation from a driver that has already turned' failure — recent comp trends are inflecting upward, but the median approach structurally cannot see that.

survived

The net sales estimate is roughly plausible as a sequential/seasonal baseline since it's anchored to a consistent, recent, verified Q1 FY2026 actual, and the general philosophy of using shrunk medians to avoid overfitting to noisy single quarters is methodologically sound as a baseline device.

broke

The EPS estimate is built on a series that appears to mix incompatible bases (full-year vs. quarterly, and a large negative outlier likely from an impairment), making the growth-rate math unreliable regardless of the shrinkage applied. The comparable-sales estimate ignores clear recent momentum acceleration and instead reverts to a stale long-run median, likely underestimating the current trend. The net sales estimate also risks missing quarter-to-quarter seasonality since it doesn't explicitly account for Q2 being seasonally stronger than Q1/Q4.

guidancestated 0.3833 → survived 0.22 · eroded 0.16
argued

The lens correctly recognizes that HD's point guidance (midpoint of a range) is not a reliable unbiased predictor of actuals, and tries to correct for systematic optimism bias by using a historical landing-position fraction. This is a legitimate methodological instinct — companies often guide conservatively-optimistic and land toward the low end, and adjusting for that bias rather than naively taking the midpoint is a reasonable improvement. The most weight-bearing evidence is the FY2025 case itself (HD-084 guided 1.0% vs HD-052 actual 0.3%), which is a real, verifiable instance of guidance overshoot, and applying it consistently across sales, EPS, and comp sales shows methodological discipline rather than cherry-picking.

attacked

The entire framework rests on a single historical data point (one year's guided range vs. one year's actual), from which a precise 'landing fraction' of ~0.15 is extracted and then applied with false precision across three different metrics (sales, EPS, comps). One observation cannot establish a stable 'landing fraction' — it could be idiosyncratic to FY2025's specific conditions (e.g., a tariff shock, weak home-improvement demand cycle) rather than a persistent structural tendency of HD's guidance process. Additionally, there's a basis mismatch: the 0.15 fraction was derived from comp-sales guidance vs. actual, but is then applied unchanged to total sales growth and to EPS growth — three different metrics with different volatility, different drivers (e.g., EPS also depends on buybacks, margin, tax rate, SRS Distribution acquisition contribution), and no evidence the same bias fraction transfers across them. The EPS estimate additionally assumes comp-sales landing dynamics translate proportionally to EPS growth, which ignores that EPS guidance already embeds different assumptions (leverage, interest expense, share count) that don't move in lockstep with comp sales. There is also a quarter-vs-annual mismatch: the entire estimate is an annual growth rate mechanically applied to a single quarter's base, with no seasonality adjustment for Q2 specifically — the lens admits this is 'rough' but still reports point estimates without wide error bars. Finally, the reasoning method would produce roughly the same qualitative conclusion (low-end landing) regardless of what evidence is available, since it's built on an assumed persistent conservative-bias story that isn't tested against disconfirming years.

survived

The qualitative insight that guidance midpoints tend to overstate outcomes and that a low-end lean is a reasonable prior going into FY2026 remains plausible and is explicitly acknowledged as fragile by the lens itself (stated confidence is already low, 0.35-0.4). The directional signal (sales/comps/EPS likely near the low end of guided ranges rather than midpoint) is defensible as a qualitative heuristic.

broke

The specific numeric point estimates (46565, 4.71, 0.3) rely on a single-observation-derived fraction applied across three distinct metrics and from annual to quarterly basis without adjustment — this precision is not supportable. The cross-metric transfer of the 0.15 fraction (from comp sales to total sales and to EPS) is unjustified and likely the weakest link, since EPS is influenced by many factors independent of comp-sales landing behavior.

driversstated 0.5 → survived 0.35 · eroded 0.15
argued

This is a well-structured driver decomposition that ties every estimate back to management's own guidance ranges and the most recent actual quarter (Q1 FY2026), rather than a black-box top-down number. For net sales, it correctly notes Q1 ran hotter than the full-year guidance midpoint (4.8% vs 3.5%) and reasonably interpolates a deceleration path, landing on ~4% growth off a clean prior-year comp base ($45.277B). For total comp sales, decomposing into transactions vs. ticket is the right granularity, and citing the multi-quarter comp trajectory (-0.3%, +1.0%, +0.2%, +0.4%, +0.6%) shows genuine attention to the trend rather than a single anchor point. The strongest piece of evidence is the Q1 FY2026 transaction/ticket split (-1.3%/+2.2%), which is a real, current, granular signal about the demand mix driving the top line, and it's used consistently across both the net sales and comp sales estimates — good internal coherence.

attacked

The EPS chain contains an internal contradiction the lens doesn't resolve: full-year adjusted EPS guidance (flat to +4% off $14.69) mechanically requires H2 to show meaningful improvement over Q1's -3.7% YoY decline, since Q1 alone was down sharply and three more quarters need to average out to flat-or-better for the year. Yet the lens explicitly extrapolates 'similar magnitude of YoY pressure as Q1 (roughly -2% to -4%)' into Q2 — this contradicts the very guidance it cites as an anchor, rather than reconciling with it. If Q2 continued at -3.7%, hitting even flat full-year growth would require an implausible H2 snapback that the lens never models. Separately, the comp sales estimate treats the Q2 FY2025 base as just another data point in a smoothly improving trend, but the historical sequence itself shows Q2 FY25 (+1.0%) was a discrete outlier bump surrounded by lower quarters (-0.3%, +0.2%, +0.4%) — meaning Q2 FY26 faces a harder YoY comparison than the adjacent quarters did, which cuts against simply reverting to the full-year guided midpoint. The net sales growth rate selection (~4%, 'between guidance midpoint and Q1 actual') is also an unprincipled interpolation — there's no structural driver given for why deceleration should land exactly there rather than, say, holding near Q1's 4.8% (if spring demand carried through) or falling toward 3.5% (if it didn't). Finally, Q2 is seasonally HD's highest-margin quarter (peak spring/summer sales mix), and the lens's flat extrapolation of margin pressure doesn't address whether normal seasonal mix effects would independently move margins regardless of YoY macro trends.

survived

The core mechanical framework — decomposing sales into prior-year base times growth rate, and comps into transactions plus ticket — is sound and appropriately transparent. The directional call (modest positive comp, continued but decelerating EPS pressure, sales growth near guidance) is plausible and the confidence levels (0.55, 0.45, 0.5) are honestly modest, already reflecting real uncertainty rather than false precision.

broke

The specific point estimates rely on unprincipled interpolation choices (why ~4% and not another point in the range) and the EPS estimate is internally inconsistent with the full-year guidance arithmetic it cites — extrapolating Q1's decline forward while also citing guidance that implies H2 recovery is a genuine logical gap, not just noise. The comp sales estimate's 'reversion to trend' framing glosses over the fact that Q2 FY25 was itself an anomalously strong quarter, making the YoY comparison harder than the adjacent-quarter trend implies.

demandstated 0.05 → survived 0.55
argued

The lens is disciplined about its mandate: forecasting demand-side variables (net sales, EPS, comp sales) properly requires independent evidence of downstream customer spending (housing starts, remodeling activity, Pro contractor capex) and upstream supplier volumes, not just HD's self-reported results. Since the evidence store contains only HD's own financials and guidance, the lens correctly identifies that using those to make a 'demand' forecast would just be relabeling the Guidance lens's work as something else. Abstaining with low stated confidence is intellectually honest and avoids the common failure mode of dressing up derivative reasoning as independent analysis. The clearest evidence for this stance is the total absence of housing-market, contractor-backlog, or supplier-shipment data in the corpus — a structural gap, not a matter of interpretation.

attacked

The abstention conflates 'no independent primary-source demand data' with 'no demand-relevant evidence at all.' HD's own reported comp sales, sales growth, and guidance are not merely 'the company talking about itself' — they are the direct, observable output of downstream demand, since Home Depot's transactions ARE the demand-side signal from millions of customers and contractors. A Demand lens could and arguably should use realized comp-sales trends, ticket vs. transaction splits, and category performance (if present) as revealed-preference evidence of customer/contractor behavior, cross-checked against known macro conditions (mortgage rates, existing home sales, housing turnover) which are general knowledge even if not explicitly cited in the evidence store. Total abstention with zero directional view is arguably an overcorrection: the lens had material figures (comp sales +0.6%, sales of $41.8B) that speak directly to demand strength/weakness, and refusing to even characterize whether demand looks soft, flat, or firming (rather than giving a point estimate) forgoes legitimate inference. Also, the claim that this is 'the Guidance lens's domain' assumes a rigid lens taxonomy where reported actuals belong exclusively to Guidance — but reported comp sales are backward-looking realized demand, categorically different from forward guidance, and a Demand lens ignoring them entirely may be applying an overly narrow self-definition rather than a principled epistemic constraint.

survived

The core observation that the evidence store lacks independent value-chain data (contractor capex, housing starts, supplier shipments) is accurate, and full point-estimate forecasting of net sales/EPS/comps without that data would indeed be ungrounded. The abstention is a defensible, low-risk choice given the stated mandate.

broke

The lens's total refusal to even qualitatively characterize demand direction using the realized comp-sales/sales figures overstates the case for abstention — those figures are legitimate (if imperfect) demand signals, not solely 'Guidance lens' territory, and a middle path (low-confidence directional read) was available but not taken. The lens's self-imposed mandate boundary may be stricter than epistemically necessary.

marketstated 0.3 → survived 0.28 · eroded 0.02

The lens is intellectually honest about a real limitation: it has no independent market-sizing data (Census retail sales, NAHB indices, housing turnover) and refuses to launder HD's own guidance as if it were an external market benchmark — that's a legitimate methodological scruple, since using guidance as 'market growth' would be circular. Given that constraint, it does the next best thing: extrapolates from HD's own recent quarterly trajectory (Q1 FY26 +4.8% sales, +0.6% comps) and full-year guidance bands, cross-checks against the model's own reproduction error, and explicitly discounts a model output that conflates annual/quarterly EPS scale. The self-assigned low confidence (0.25-0.35) is well-calibrated to the acknowledged evidence gap. The most load-bearing piece of evidence is the Q1 FY2026 actual print (+4.8% sales, +0.6% comps), since it's the most recent real data point closest to the target period, rather than stale prior-year comparisons.

attacked

Despite being labeled a 'market' lens, this analysis contains zero independent market data — it is pure company-trend extrapolation dressed in market-lens clothing, making it largely redundant with whatever a trend/guidance lens would produce, not a genuine market-vs-share decomposition. Several internal inconsistencies also weaken it: (1) Q1 FY2026 sales growth was 4.8% YoY, notably above the full-year guidance midpoint of ~3.5%, implying an expected deceleration through the year to hit guidance — yet the lens applies a flat 3.5%-4.5% rate to Q2 as if Q1 momentum simply continues, without addressing why deceleration wouldn't apply sooner. (2) For EPS, the lens computes a 1.5%-2.5% growth range applied to $4.68, which mechanically yields $4.75-$4.80, but then anchors on the low end ($4.75) without justification given that comps and sales both point to accelerating, not decelerating, momentum. (3) For comps, it averages in a model estimate (0.2%) explicitly flagged as unreliable (-138% reproduction error) into a 0.5%-1.0% range, which is incoherent — either discount it fully or don't cite it as supporting evidence. (4) The lens never engages with macro data that actually was available and would count as genuine 'market' evidence (e.g., existing home sales levels, remodeling spend proxies, interest rate environment) — it treats the absence of Census/NAHB series as absence of all market context, when readily known macro headwinds (elevated mortgage rates suppressing housing turnover) could have informed a very different market-growth read. (5) The quarter-over-quarter seasonal analog (Q2 FY2025 base × growth rate) assumes stable seasonality, but no evidence is presented that FY2026 seasonal patterns match FY2025 (e.g., tariff-driven pull-forward buying, promotional calendar shifts).

survived

The core numerical extrapolation is plausible and internally roughly consistent with HD's own guidance bands and recent trajectory — $46.9B sales, ~$4.75 EPS, and ~0.7% comps are not unreasonable central estimates given the cited data. The lens's transparency about its own limitations and its explicit statement of what would change its mind are genuine strengths that should be preserved.

broke

The claim to being a distinct 'market' perspective does not hold — it is company-trend extrapolation with no market decomposition, so it shouldn't be weighted as an independent corroborating view. The specific point estimates (especially the low-end EPS anchor and the comps range incorporating a flagged-unreliable model output) rest on somewhat arbitrary choices rather than defensible logic, and the implicit assumption of steady momentum from Q1 to Q2 ignores the deceleration implied by full-year guidance math.

peer_readstated 0.05 → survived 0.55
argued

This is a disciplined, methodologically honest abstention. The lens's entire mandate is to provide a peer-based read-across, and it correctly identifies that the evidence corpus contains zero comparable-company data points (no Lowe's, no other big-box retailer prints) overlapping HD's FY2026Q2. Rather than dress up an extrapolation from HD's own filings as a 'peer read' — which would be a category error, smuggling a self-referential trend analysis under a peer-comparison label — it abstains across all three metrics (net sales, adjusted EPS, comps) with low stated confidence and clearly states what evidence would change its mind. This is exactly the right behavior for a lens: knowing the boundary of its own evidence base and not manufacturing false signal. The strongest piece of evidence is simply the negative one — the absence of any peer citations anywhere in the three writeups — which is itself verifiable by inspecting the evidence store cited (HD-001, HD-006, HD-169 are all HD's own filings).

attacked

The abstention may be too absolute and could be masking a weaker but still real capability. First, 'no peer data in the evidence corpus' is a statement about this particular evidence store, not about the world — the lens conflates 'I was not given peer data' with 'no peer read is possible,' when in fact public, contemporaneous Lowe's/big-box data almost certainly exists and a more resourceful lens might flag that the gap is a curation failure rather than a true absence of signal, and could still offer a soft qualitative read (e.g., 'sector-wide, home improvement demand has been described as soft amid high rates' from general knowledge) rather than full abstention. Second, applying identical 0.05 confidence and identical reasoning to three quite different metrics (net sales, EPS, comps) is a red flag: the same boilerplate abstention was produced regardless of whether the metric was top-line, margin-driven, or comp-based — suggesting the lens isn't actually evaluating each metric's peer-sensitivity individually but running a single templated check-for-peer-citations gate. Third, abstention is not free — a peer lens that abstains on every quarter it's asked about provides zero value across the board, and if this is a pattern rather than a one-off gap, it suggests the evidence-provisioning process (not the lens) is broken, which the abstention framing doesn't surface as sharply as it could. Finally, the lens claims high honesty but doesn't quantify how confident it is that no peer data exists somewhere in a fuller corpus — it's making an absence claim without proving exhaustive search.

survived

The core discipline — refusing to relabel a self-referential HD-only trend extrapolation as a 'peer read' — is sound and the right call given the stated evidence constraints. The abstention is transparent, falsifiable (states exactly what would change its mind), and internally consistent across all three metrics.

broke

The uniformity of the abstention (same confidence, same boilerplate reasoning) across three distinct metrics suggests a templated gate rather than metric-specific judgment, and the lens doesn't distinguish between 'peer data doesn't exist' versus 'peer data wasn't provided to me,' nor does it attempt any lower-confidence qualitative peer-sector context that could still add marginal value instead of pure abstention.

What the judge did.
Net sales (USDm)

Weighted the driver/margins/forensics cluster's construction — prior-year Q2 base of $45,277M grown ~4% — most heavily, not because three lenses landed there but because each independently rebuilt the number from the two things that actually determine it: the seasonally correct year-ago quarter and the realized Q1 FY2026 growth rate of +4.8%, which still carries inorganic contribution that does not anniversary until later in the year. That construction also reconciles internally: comps near +0.9% plus acquisition/new-store contribution plus modest ticket inflation lands at ~4.2% growth, i.e. ~$47.1-47.2B. The mechanical lens ($41,835M) was set aside outright — it is carrying the Q1 absolute level forward and so misses the largest seasonal step in HD's year; the forensics lens flagged exactly this base-period mismatch, and the metric's stated 1-sigma swing of $28.4bn confirms the history series is not a usable scale reference here. The view I was most tempted by was the guidance lens's $46,565M, built on a defensible landing-position argument that HD historically prints near the low end of its guided ranges (FY2025: guided ~1.0% comp, actual 0.3%); I gave it real weight in setting the lower half of the interval but not the median, because that landing fraction is estimated off a single guidance-vs-actual pair and it argues against an already-realized Q1 print of +4.8%. Interval widened on the low side to accommodate that low-end-landing risk and because both demand and peer lenses abstained, leaving no independent read on end-market turnover or a competitor's comp.

weighting: Materiality: net sales is the metric where a mis-specified base period costs several billion dollars, so weight went to views that used the seasonally correct year-ago quarter and reconciled top-line growth to its components; views whose numbers moved only with an assumed growth rate applied to a wrong base earned near-zero weight regardless of stated confidence.

Adjusted diluted EPS (USD / share)

This is the widest genuine disagreement in economic terms and I split it deliberately rather than picking a camp. The margins and forensics lenses ($4.51 and $4.50) rest on the single most material observable: Q1 FY2026 adjusted EPS fell 3.7% YoY with adjusted operating margin compressing to 12.3% from 13.2%, and full-year gross margin guided at ~33.1% against an adjusted operating margin guide of 12.8-13.0% below the prior year's realized level. That is a mechanism, not an extrapolation, and forensics adds a corroborating detail with teeth — the GAAP-to-adjusted operating margin spread has narrowed to ~0.4pt from ~0.9-1.0pt, so fewer costs are being excluded, making the adjusted figure harder to flatter. Against that, the guidance/macro/market cluster at $4.71-4.75 leans on management's own flat-to-+4% full-year frame off $14.69, which arithmetically requires the remaining quarters to run +1% to +6% after a down Q1. Both cannot be right for Q2, and the honest read is that Q2 sits between a repeat of Q1's decline and the improvement guidance implies — roughly flat YoY versus $4.68. I centered at $4.62. Most tempted by the margins lens's $4.51, and set it aside only because it assumes Q1's compression magnitude repeats unchanged into a quarter with easier opex leverage on a much larger sales base. The mechanical projection of $4.33 is discounted heavily: its own measured reproduction error is -18.7%, which is larger than the entire spread between the surviving views. Band kept wide (p10-p90 ~53c) because demand abstained on input costs/tariffs and peer_read abstained entirely, so nothing independent constrains the margin path.

weighting: Materiality: EPS turns on adjusted operating margin, so weight went to the views that cited actual margin levels and the guidance arithmetic they must satisfy. The mechanical view was discounted by its own 18.7% reproduction error, which is material relative to the disagreement being adjudicated.

Comparable sales, total company (%)

Centered at +0.9%, just below the full-year guided midpoint of ~1.0% and above the realized Q1 print of +0.6%. The driver lens carried the most weight because it is the only view that decomposed the number into its actual components — Q1 comparable transactions -1.3% against average ticket +2.2% — and then placed that decomposition inside the improving sequential path (-0.3%, +1.0%, +0.2%, +0.4%, +0.6%). Forensics sharpened the same evidence in the opposite direction, correctly noting that negative traffic with positive ticket is price/mix carrying the print rather than demand, which is why I did not push the median to the guided midpoint despite the tougher +1.0% year-ago base. The guidance lens's +0.3%, built on the FY2025 low-end-landing precedent, is the view I was most tempted by and it substantially set my p10-p25; I declined to make it the median because the landing fraction comes from one observation and Q1 has already printed above that path. The mechanical +0.2% is effectively uninformative here — the reported reproduction error of -138% on this series says the extrapolation does not reproduce its own history. This is by far the widest relative band of the three (CoV among views 0.21) and I widened it further: comps routinely surprise by a full point, and the two abstentions are precisely the lenses that would have constrained this metric — demand on remodeling/housing turnover and peer_read on a competitor's comp print. Silence there is a gap, not confirmation, so the low tail admits a negative comp and the high tail reaches the top of guidance.

weighting: Materiality: with a 1-sigma historical swing of only ~0.41pt, the whole live range spans several sigma, so weight went to the view that built the number from transactions and ticket rather than from a level average; the two abstentions bear directly on this metric and were converted into interval width, not ignored.

Absent views were named to it, not hidden: Two lenses abstained and both abstentions were honest and material. lens_demand would have supplied the downstream/upstream link — remodeling spend indices, contractor backlogs, housing turnover, and supplier shipment or input-cost data — which is the only independent check on whether comps and ticket inflation are demand-driven or price-driven, and the only outside read on tariff/commodity pressure feeding the margin line. lens_peer_read would have given a genuine cross-company read on end-market demand (a home-improvement peer's comparable sales, traffic-versus-ticket mix and margin trend over an overlapping period), which is the standard way to test whether HD's guided flat-to-+2.0% comp band is conservative or optimistic. Their absence means every surviving view is ultimately anchored on Home Depot's own reported history and its own guidance, so the views are less independent of each other than the count of seven suggests. I widened the comparable-sales interval on both tails and extended the low tail on adjusted EPS accordingly, rather than reading the two abstentions as agreement with the remaining cluster.

argue, attack, survive — per lens
mechanicalstated 0.5 → survived 0.28 · eroded 0.22
argued

The mechanical, no-judgement approach is the best kind of honest baseline: it is transparent about method, cites its actual data points, and doesn't pretend a model call adds precision it can't earn. For revenue, taking the most recent reported quarter as an anchor and applying a shrunk (regularized) median growth rate is a defensible way to avoid overreacting to noisy YoY spikes while still capturing the recent uptrend (2880→3076→3160). The EPS series is the most persuasive piece of evidence here: 1.85→2.05→3.09 over roughly a year shows a real, large earnings inflection consistent with a semiconductor upcycle, and extrapolating further growth from that trajectory is a reasonable mechanical read given no contradicting information.

attacked

The three sub-forecasts are not built on a consistent information set, and that inconsistency exposes the model's weakness. The EPS citations already include an actual for 'Three Months Ended May 2, 2026: 3.09' — i.e., an actual quarter *after* the revenue series' last cited point (Jan 31, 2026: 3160). Yet the revenue forecast for the same future quarter is only 3160.29, essentially flat versus the January actual, while EPS and margin forecasts are built as if extrapolating forward from an already more advanced actual base. This is a basis mismatch: different lines of the same forecast are anchored at different points in time, which will produce an internally inconsistent revenue/EPS/margin triangle (e.g. margin × revenue won't reconcile to the implied EPS growth). Worse, the gross margin call is actively contradicted by the model's own cited evidence: the three data points shown are 69.8, 71.2, and 73.0 — a clear, monotonic upward trend — yet the 'shrunk median of level' forecast lands at 69.2, *below* every one of the three most recent actuals and even below the oldest of the three. A methodology that produces a forecast lower than the most recent three consecutive actuals, when those actuals show a clean upward trend, is not capturing the current regime; it's being dragged down by stale history from earlier, weaker periods and the shrinkage is doing more work than the recent trend deserves. Similarly, the EPS growth extrapolation assumes the median growth rate from a 9-period window continues, but a chunk of that window likely reflects the post-downturn earnings trough-to-recovery snapback (1.85 as a low base), which is a one-time low-base effect, not a sustainable forward growth rate — extrapolating it forward is extrapolating a decelerating base effect as if it were structural.

survived

The core method — anchoring to the latest actual and applying a regularized (shrunk) growth/level rate rather than a raw naive extrapolation — is a reasonable, honest baseline with appropriately modest stated confidence (0.5). The EPS trajectory as raw evidence of an earnings upcycle is real and not in dispute.

broke

The gross margin forecast is internally contradicted by its own cited evidence (forecast below all three most recent actuals despite a clear upward trend), indicating the shrinkage/median approach is stale and not regime-aware. The three metrics (revenue, EPS, margin) appear anchored at different historical cutoffs, creating a mismatch that undermines coherence across the joint forecast. The EPS growth extrapolation risks conflating a low-base recovery snapback with sustainable forward growth.

guidancestated 0.4833 → survived 0.5
argued

The lens does the epistemically honest thing: it anchors on explicit, dated management guidance for revenue and adjusted EPS rather than inventing an independent forecast, and it correctly distinguishes GAAP EPS guidance from adjusted EPS guidance (a distinction lenses often blur). For gross margin, where no direct guidance exists, it builds a transparent bridge from adjusted operating margin using the most recent quarter's AOM-AGM spread, and it explicitly flags this as inference rather than fact, with correspondingly lower confidence (0.3 vs 0.6/0.55). The confidence calibration direction is sound: highest confidence where evidence is most direct (a stated guidance range), lowest where it required an inferential leap. The single most load-bearing piece of evidence is the literal guidance quotes [ADI-102, ADI-106], which are about as strong as forward-looking evidence gets for a next-quarter estimate.

attacked

Several weaknesses. First, treating the guided midpoint as an unbiased estimate is itself a judgment call dressed up as a default — semiconductor companies, including ADI historically, are well-documented to guide with a systematic conservative tilt so they can beat on the print; the lens's absence-of-evidence framing ('no historical pairs available') is used to justify inaction, but the more defensible prior (informed by well-known industry behavior, not just ADI's own data) would skew slightly above the midpoint, not sit at it. Second, the gross margin bridge is built on a single quarter's AOM-AGM spread (24pts from Q2 FY26) despite the lens's own claim that the gap has ranged 24-28pts and is 'narrowing' — that's an unsubstantiated trend assertion resting on one or two data points, and the resulting 72.5% figure inherits all of that fragility while being presented as a specific number with only modestly discounted confidence (0.3, arguably still too high for a chained inference with no direct support). Third, essentially the entire revenue and EPS analysis amounts to restating company guidance with a confidence label attached — this isn't independent forecasting, it's reading the letter, and calling it 0.6/0.55 confidence may overstate what predictive work has actually been done versus just parroting a press release, especially given semis are exposed to short-cycle demand/tariff shocks that can move revenue away from guidance within a quarter.

survived

The core mechanical approach — anchoring on explicit direct guidance for revenue and adjusted EPS, keeping GAAP and adjusted EPS separate, and being transparent that the gross margin figure is a derived inference with correspondingly lower stated confidence — is methodologically sound and honestly presented. The relative confidence ordering (direct guidance > inferred bridge) is defensible.

broke

The claim of no landing-position bias is not actually neutral; it's a substantive assumption that ignores general (non-ADI-specific) knowledge of guidance-beat patterns in the semiconductor sector, which the lens could have incorporated as a soft prior even without ADI-specific historical pairs. The gross margin bridge's stated 24-28pt range and 'narrowing' trend is not adequately evidenced — it looks like it's inferred from very few observations, undermining the reliability of the resulting 72.5% figure beyond what a 0.3 confidence already discounts.

The single most load-bearing piece of evidence is the guidance quote itself [ADI-102]/[ADI-106], since company guidance issued near quarter-end is generally the best predictor of the print, far better than naive time-series extrapolation.

The revenue and EPS 'estimates' are not really independent driver-based forecasts — they are restatements of management guidance with a thin narrative wrapper, so the 0.6ish confidence is doing little epistemic work beyond 'management said so.' More seriously, the gross margin call (73.8%, extrapolated +0.5–1.0pt above 73.0%) is built on a logical gap: guided operating margin is flat sequentially at ~49%, which is at least as consistent with flat-to-declining gross margin (offset by opex leverage) as with rising gross margin. The lens asserts utilization gains should lift gross margin further, but the same utilization/volume growth has already decelerated sharply (14.6%→7.6% seq), which should mechanically slow the pace of margin expansion, not sustain it. There's also a mix risk explicitly acknowledged but not weighted: Comms/Consumer recovery could be dragging mix down even as absolute volumes rise. Finally, the historical margin trajectory cited (68.8→69.2→69.8→71.2→73.0) shows a monotonic climb of varying step sizes with no structural reason given for why 73.5–74% specifically is the next step rather than a plateau near 73%, given flat op-margin guidance — this is an extrapolation from a short, decelerating trend dressed up as a driver-based derivation.

survived

The revenue ($3.9B) and EPS ($3.30) figures remain well-supported since they are directly sourced from management's stated guidance, which is the most reliable near-term anchor available absent independent channel data. The overall recovery narrative (utilization improving off trough, sequential growth normalizing) is plausible and consistent with the cited trend data.

broke

The gross margin extrapolation to 73.5–74% does not actually follow from the flat 49% operating margin guidance — that guidance is equally consistent with flat or even slightly compressed gross margin offset by opex discipline. The reasoning also glosses over the fact that the revenue growth deceleration undercuts the utilization-driven margin-expansion thesis it leans on, making the specific +0.5-1.0pt bump under-justified relative to a 'roughly flat near 73%' alternative.

demandstated 0.05 → survived 0.35
argued

The lens correctly identifies that its mandate is specifically demand-side/value-chain triangulation (customer capex, supplier wafer volumes) and that the evidence corpus contains none of that — only ADI's own guidance and historical self-reported figures. Rather than dress up a guess as demand-grounded analysis, it abstains across all three metrics (revenue, adjusted EPS, adjusted gross margin) for the same stated reason, which is internally consistent and epistemically disciplined. The strongest piece of evidence for this position is simply the negative finding itself: every citation offered (ADI-102, ADI-106, ADI-005) is company-sourced, and the lens explicitly declines to launder that into an 'independent' read, correctly noting that reusing self-reported guidance as if it were value-chain confirmation would be a basis mismatch (treating company guidance as demand evidence). Its articulation of what would change its mind (specific customer/supplier disclosures) shows the abstention is falsifiable and not just reflexive caution.

attacked

The abstention is defensible on narrow methodological grounds but may be too rigid/uninformative in practice. First, absence of named customer/supplier disclosures does not mean zero demand-side signal exists in the corpus — semiconductor industry demand conditions (SOX index trends, distributor sell-through, book-to-bill ratios) are often embedded indirectly in company commentary even if not separately sourced; the lens may be applying an overly strict evidentiary bar that guarantees abstention regardless of what's actually knowable, which is itself a red flag ('reasoning that would produce the same answer regardless of evidence') — if the corpus literally never contains third-party customer/supplier data by construction, this lens will always abstain, making it uninformative as a lens rather than a genuine finding for this specific quarter. Second, guidance itself (ADI-102, ADI-106) is not pure company narrative — it's management's own aggregation of order backlog and customer conversations, which indirectly encodes demand information; dismissing it entirely as 'not value-chain evidence' throws out signal that, while not independent, is not worthless either. Third, the uniform 0.05 confidence across three quite different metrics (revenue, EPS, gross margin) suggests a templated non-answer rather than metric-specific reasoning — gross margin, for instance, could be informed by product mix and cost trends that ADI discloses in more granular fashion than pure top-line demand, yet the same boilerplate abstention is applied without differentiation.

survived

The core observation — that the evidence store lacks independent customer/supplier disclosures and that ADI's own guidance is being used as the only input — is factually accurate and the lens's refusal to relabel company guidance as demand-side evidence is methodologically sound.

broke

The uniformity and mechanical nature of the abstention across three distinct metrics suggests the lens's decision rule is invariant to the evidence at hand (it would abstain identically regardless of what ADI's guidance said), which limits its practical value; also the claim that guidance carries zero demand information is overstated since guidance is itself downstream of management's read of customer demand.

marketstated 0.4 → survived 0.4
argued

The lens is honest about its central limitation: it has no independent market data, so it cannot decompose ADI's growth into market-cycle vs share-gain components, and it flags this repeatedly rather than pretending otherwise. Given that constraint, using company guidance as the anchor for revenue ($3.9B) and EPS ($3.30) is the most defensible choice available — guidance is typically well-calibrated near-term (management has visibility into backlog/bookings for the current quarter) and is corroborated by a consistent sequential trend (Q2 FY26 $3.62B revenue, $3.09 EPS climbing from $2.05 y/y). The gross margin call is the sharpest piece of reasoning here: rather than accepting a stale model output (69.2%) that lags the observed trajectory (68.8%→69.2%→71.2%→73.0%), the lens correctly identifies the trend and extrapolates the most recent actual (73.0%) instead of a shrunk median that ignores the recent inflection. That's a good catch — the model residual is clearly out of date relative to the reported trend.

attacked

Several structural issues. First, on gross margin: extrapolating a rising sequential trend by simply carrying the most recent print forward (73.0%) is not really an estimate — it assumes zero mean-reversion and zero seasonality, and four data points of a monotonic rise is too thin a base to justify holding flat rather than expecting continued incremental improvement or a slight give-back (utilization/mix swings quarter to quarter are common in analog semis). The lens presents this as 'extrapolation' but it's actually just anchoring on last-quarter-actual, which is a different (weaker) claim than genuine trend extrapolation. Second, and more importantly, the revenue and EPS estimates are literally just restating management's own guidance midpoint with no independent adjustment — the lens's discussion of 'circularity' is acknowledged but never actually addressed; it doesn't attempt any correction, sanity check, or triangulation (e.g., cross-checking guidance against historical guidance-to-actual beat/miss patterns, which ADI and most semis do have a history of beating). That omission means the 'confidence' figures (0.45, 0.40, 0.35) are somewhat theatrical — they gesture at epistemic humility but the actual point estimates are unadjusted guidance/last-actual, so the confidence discount isn't doing any real work in the number itself. Third, semiconductor cycles are known for sharp inflections; a company guiding off a strong two-quarter run could be guiding into a peak, and the lens has no mechanism to detect that risk since it explicitly disclaims macro/cycle awareness. Given ADI's history of cyclicality (2022-2023 downturn), 'up sharply, consistent with trend' is exactly the kind of framing that fails right before a turn.

survived

The core epistemic stance — that without independent market data, guidance-anchored point estimates are the best available and share/cycle attribution is genuinely unknowable — holds up. The gross margin observation that the income-model's 69.2% is stale relative to the actual reported trend is also a valid, verifiable point (the cited figures do show a clear rise).

broke

The margin 'extrapolation' is weaker than presented — it's a last-actual carry-forward dressed as trend analysis, with no accounting for mean reversion or the thinness of the four-point series. The stated confidences don't functionally differ from just trusting guidance outright, since no independent adjustment or historical guidance-accuracy check was performed to justify the confidence levels or discount the numbers at all.

marginsstated 0.6667 → survived 0.55 · eroded 0.12
argued

The lens correctly anchors on management's own explicit guidance for revenue ($3.9B ±$100M) and adjusted EPS ($3.30 ±$0.15), which is the single most authoritative and direct data point available for a forward quarter — management has visibility into backlog, bookings, and channel inventory that outside estimators lack. The gross margin derivation is a sensible bridge: using the guided operating margin (49.0%, flat vs Q2 actual) and back-solving via the observed opex ratio (~24pts) from the two most recent quarters is a defensible, mechanically transparent way to infer an unguided line item. The revenue and EPS figures carry the most evidentiary weight since they are direct quotes from management guidance, not derived — that is about as strong as single-quarter forecasting evidence gets.

attacked

The core weakness is that the gross margin figure isn't independent evidence — it's an algebraic derivation with a strong constant-opex-ratio assumption baked in, and it is presented with unearned specificity (73.0%, one decimal place) when the actual uncertainty band is much wider. The opex ratio was computed from only two data points (Q1-Q2 FY2026), which is far too few observations to establish a stable trend — a single sequential quarter's ratio could easily be noise (e.g., one-time opex timing, R&D project phasing, seasonal SG&A) rather than a structural constant. Moreover, the revenue guidance itself, sitting exactly at the guided midpoint, is essentially just restating management's number as the estimate with a 0.75 confidence — but ADI has a history of guiding conservatively and beating; taking the midpoint at face value ignores the asymmetric beat-rate pattern common in semis guidance, which would matter if the estimand is actual revenue rather than 'what management said.' The EPS figure similarly restates guidance without independently validating whether the margin assumptions embedded in that guidance (mix, tax rate) are consistent with what's actually likely given end-market trends (e.g., auto/industrial softness that has affected other analog peers in the same period) — no external cross-check is offered. Finally, there's a subtle basis risk: adjusted operating margin flat quarter-over-quarter does not necessarily imply gross margin flat — opex could be guided down in dollar terms while gross margin also declines, and the 24pt spread could shift for reasons unrelated to what the lens flags (e.g., FX, one-time items in Q2 actual opex that don't recur, stock comp variability affecting adjusted opex ratio).

survived

The revenue and EPS numbers as restatements of management's direct guidance remain solid — they are appropriately sourced and the lens is transparent that this is essentially taking guidance at face value, which is a reasonable default absent contrary evidence. The mechanical logic of the gross margin bridge is internally consistent and clearly documented, including its own stated invalidation conditions.

broke

The gross margin estimate's precision (73.0%, single decimal) overstates what a two-quarter opex-ratio extrapolation can support; the confidence of 0.55 is still probably too high for an indirectly-derived, thinly-evidenced figure. The EPS confidence of 0.7 doesn't account for the fact that guided adjusted EPS depends on gross margin assumptions that are themselves uncertain (circular support). No consideration is given to ADI's guidance-beat history, which is directly relevant if the estimand is actual outcome rather than guidance repetition.

The narrowing-adjustment-gap argument is a reasonable check but it's an indirect proxy — it shows the exclusions aren't growing, not that the margin trend itself will continue; these are separate claims being conflated. The EPS bridge evidence is thinner than presented (two non-adjacent quarters).

The lens correctly identifies its own mandate — peer read-across — and correctly determines the evidence store has zero qualifying data to fulfill that mandate. It resists the temptation to substitute ADI's own guidance for genuine peer disclosure, which would be a basis mismatch (restating the subject company's own forecast as if it were independent corroborating evidence). This is methodologically disciplined: abstention is the epistemically honest move when the specific input a method requires is simply absent, rather than forcing an output through a proxy that violates the method's own logic. The abstention is defensible as far as it goes, but it may be too rigid in how it defines 'peer data.' A sophisticated read-across lens could still function partially by using proxy signals even absent literal peer earnings releases — e.g., known industry-wide semiconductor cycle indicators, macro data (PMI, semiconductor billings indices), or even indirect mentions of end-market conditions embedded in ADI's own MD&A commentary about customer inventory or channel dynamics, which often reflect broader industry trends analysts use for read-across in absence of direct peer prints. The lens treats 'no peer disclosure in corpus' as equivalent to 'no basis for any peer-informed view,' but that conflates unavailability of ideal evidence with unavailability of all evidence. Additionally, the claim that peer data is completely absent from the corpus is itself unverified — the lens states this based on its own search but doesn't demonstrate exhaustive checking (e.g., no mention of SIA data, WSTS reports, or channel checks that might exist elsewhere in the store). The abstention outcome is reasonable given the stated strict definition of 'peer data' and the lens's honest disclosure of what would change its mind.

broke

attacked

The core problem is that this lens is not really a 'macro' view at all — it's an unweighted restatement of management guidance dressed up as independent analysis, and it says so itself ('no independent macro series is wired in'). That's a critical admission: a macro lens with no macro data is not adding information beyond what guidance already provides, yet it assigns moderate confidence (0.4–0.6) as though independent verification occurred. Second, guidance is systematically optimistic-biased in upcycles and companies almost always guide to what they believe achievable, not a true expected value — treating the midpoint as the best estimate ignores the asymmetric risk of semiconductor cyclical air-pockets, which are common and can turn quickly (channel inventory corrections in this sector have historically been sharp, e.g., 2022-2023). Third, the gross margin extrapolation is particularly fragile: it explicitly rejects a 'stale shrunk-median' model in favor of the two most recent quarters' trend, which is an extrapolation from far too few observations (essentially 2-3 points) projected forward through a beat-and-raise cycle — mix shift and utilization gains at cyclical peaks are exactly where margin deceleration risk is highest, not lowest. Fourth, there's a circularity: EPS guidance, gross margin guidance, and revenue guidance are not independent — they're all issued by the same management team based on the same internal view, so citing three guidance-consistent numbers as reinforcing each other is not triangulation, it's the same data point counted three times. Finally, the 'what would change my mind' section reveals the lens has no actual mechanism to detect the failure modes it names (air-pocket, FX move, inventory correction) before the fact — it's a passive acceptance of guidance with a hypothetical off-ramp that isn't actually monitored.

survived

The overall point estimates (revenue ~3900, EPS ~3.3) are reasonable central estimates given they mirror explicit, recent management guidance, and the directional read (continued sequential growth) is well-supported by multiple quarters of consistent trend data. The acknowledgment of its own limitation (no macro data) is honest and appropriately lowers stated confidence somewhat.

broke

The framing of this as three semi-independent estimates with distinct confidence levels doesn't hold — they are effectively one guidance-derived scenario restated three times, so the appearance of convergent evidence is illusory. The gross margin estimate specifically over-extrapolates from very few data points at what could be a cyclical peak, and the discounting of the 'stale' model prior removes a useful hedge against optimism bias. Confidence levels (0.4-0.6) overstate the independence and robustness of the analysis relative to what is essentially a guidance pass-through with no verification layer.

What the judge did.
Revenue (USDm)

lens_guidance and lens_margins carried the most weight because they rest on an explicit, company-issued Q3 FY2026 revenue guide of $3.9B \u00b1 $100M — a management build/ship plan locked before the quarter closed, which is the single most material piece of evidence and the only one whose failure would move the number more than a fraction of a sigma. Six other lenses converge on $3.9B, but that convergence is not independent: lens_market, lens_macro, lens_drivers and lens_forensics each say explicitly they are anchoring on the same guidance because no third-party demand, peer, or macro series exists in the corpus — so I treated them as one piece of evidence, not six. I was most tempted by lens_mechanical's $3,160m (it is the only genuinely non-circular read), but set it aside: it extrapolates from a stale base and ignores the $3,623m Q2 print, and its own reproduction error is -6.9%, so it is mechanically anchored below the last actual — an implausible -13% sequential collapse with no supporting evidence. I shade the median ~1.2% above the guided midpoint because analog semis in an up-cycle with rising bookings conversion typically land at or above midpoint, and every lens that examined the sequential trend (2880\u21923160\u21923623) described accelerating, broad-based recovery. The band is wider than the \u00b1$100M guide on both tails because lens_demand and lens_peer_read both abstained for the same reason — zero independent end-market or competitor verification of the demand assumption underpinning the guide — so a mid-quarter demand air-pocket is unfalsifiable from this evidence.

weighting: Materiality: the guided revenue range is worth ~\u00b1$100m against a one-sigma historical swing of $318m, so the guide compresses roughly two-thirds of the metric's natural variance in one document. Nothing else in the evidence set could move revenue by a comparable amount — the mechanical model's disagreement is large in magnitude but rests on an input (stale base period, -6.9% reproduction error) that is demonstrably wrong against the last reported quarter, so its large implied swing is discounted rather than averaged in.

Adjusted diluted EPS (USD / share)

Weighted almost entirely on the explicit guide of $3.30 \u00b1 $0.15 (lens_guidance, lens_margins), which internally reconciles with the guided ~49% adjusted operating margin on $3.9B — two guided quantities that cross-check each other, which is stronger than either alone. lens_forensics added the most incremental value of any non-guidance view: it showed the GAAP-to-adjusted bridge has been shrinking ($1.01 gap in Q3FY25 to $0.69 in Q2FY26), meaning the adjusted figure is becoming less dependent on add-backs and is therefore more durable — that argues against discounting the guided adjusted number as inflated. lens_mechanical's $3.31 lands on top of guidance, but I gave it near-zero independent weight: its measured reproduction error is -20.3%, the worst of the three metrics, so its agreement is coincidence rather than corroboration and must not be read as a second confirmation. I set the median at $3.38, above the midpoint, because the EPS guide is downstream of the revenue guide and I have shaded revenue up; incremental revenue at ~73% gross margin drops through at high incrementals. The distribution is slightly left-skewed at the p10 tail to respect the possibility that the revenue guide is not met, since no independent demand check exists.

weighting: Materiality: one sigma of EPS history is $0.58 while the guided range is \u00b1$0.15 — the guide claims to narrow the distribution to about a quarter of its natural width, so it must carry nearly all the weight or nothing. The bridge that would break it is the revenue guide plus the 49% operating-margin guide; I sized the tails to how far EPS moves if revenue misses the low end (~$3.15-3.20) or beats the high end (~$3.55+), not to lens headcount.

Adjusted gross margin (%)

No lens has direct guidance here — management guided adjusted operating margin (~49%) but not gross margin, so every view is a bridge or an extrapolation, and I widened accordingly. I weighted lens_margins most: its bridge is the tightest reasoning available, taking the Q2 actual AGM 73.0% minus AOM 49.0% = ~24pt opex ratio and holding it against a flat 49% AOM guide to imply AGM near 73.0%. Against that, lens_forensics and lens_drivers make the materially better point that the series is not flat — 69.2 \u2192 69.8 \u2192 71.2 \u2192 73.0 is +1.3 to +1.8pts per quarter, and $3.9B of revenue means further utilization absorption, which mechanically lifts gross margin even if opex leverage offsets it at the operating line. I split toward the trend side at 73.4%. I was most tempted by lens_guidance's 72.5% (the low end of the surviving cluster) and set it aside because it concedes it is an inference from the same 24pt spread while arriving below the last actual print, which requires margin to go backwards despite higher volume — no lens offered a mechanism for that. lens_mechanical's 69.2% is a shrunk median of a series whose last four points are all above it and rising; it is measuring the trough, not the quarter. Note also an unresolved factual conflict in the evidence: lens_macro cites Q2 AOM as 45.5% while lens_margins and lens_guidance cite 49.0% — if the lower figure is right the opex bridge breaks entirely, which is a further reason to keep the band wide.

weighting: Materiality: one sigma is only 1.12pts, so the honest spread here (roughly 72.2-74.5) is already about two sigma wide — appropriate given this is the one metric with no direct guidance, a contested Q2 operating-margin input, and abstentions from both lenses (demand, peer_read) that would have supplied independent utilization, wafer-cost, or competitor-mix evidence. Weight went to the view with an explicit arithmetic bridge from a guided quantity, adjusted upward for the documented sequential trend that bridge assumes away.

Absent views were named to it, not hidden: Every lens produced a view, but two — lens_demand and lens_peer_read — abstained outright on all three metrics, and both abstentions are honest and material rather than neutral. lens_demand would have supplied the only non-circular check on the revenue guide: customer-side capex and budget trajectories in industrial automation, automotive electronics content, comms infrastructure, and consumer volumes, plus supplier-side foundry/wafer volume and pricing data that would independently inform gross margin. lens_peer_read would have supplied TI/Microchip/NXP/ON commentary on overlapping calendar Q2-Q3 2026 book-to-bill, lead times, and channel inventory — the classic early-warning signal for whether an analog up-cycle guide is about to be missed. Their absence means the apparent 0.0 coefficient of variation across seven views is an artifact: five of those seven state explicitly that they are restating the same company guidance for want of anything else, so the corpus contains essentially one substantive piece of evidence plus a demonstrably stale mechanical model. lens_market also flagged its own read as circular. I therefore treated the consensus as a single guidance-derived estimate, kept the revenue and EPS tails wider than the guided ranges (particularly the downside, where an unobserved end-market air-pocket or channel correction is exactly the thing the two abstaining lenses would have caught), and widened gross margin to roughly two sigma given it has no guidance at all, a contested opex bridge (Q2 AOM cited as both 49.0% and 45.5%), and no independent utilization or input-cost evidence.

What the judge did.
Net fees

Weighted almost entirely on the arithmetic that lens_drivers, lens_margins, lens_forensics, lens_market and lens_macro each built independently from a hard anchor: H1 FY26 net fees of £453.3m are actually reported, so only H2 is genuinely forecast, and H2 FY25 is a known £476.4m residual off FY25's £972.4m. Applying the disclosed Q3 -8%/Q4 -5% LFL trend to that base gives H2 of £438-448m and a full year of £895-900m. The convergence is not vote-counting — the views share one arithmetic backbone, but that backbone rests on disclosed figures rather than judgement, which is why it dominates. lens_mechanical's -7.5 is a scale artefact (its own series is contaminated: 39.9% reproduction error, a projection three orders of magnitude off the reported base) and carries no weight. The residual uncertainty is mostly FX translation on a business with large Germany/ANZ exposure and the exact split between LFL and reported fees, which is worth a few percent rather than tens — hence a band of roughly ±1.5-2%, wider on the downside because the two abstaining lenses (demand, peer_read) would have been the ones to flag an end-market deterioration in H2 that Hays' own Q4 commentary would understate.

weighting: Materiality: H1 is a reported actual covering ~50% of the metric, so only the H2 half is at risk; a 3-percentage-point error on the H2 LFL rate moves the full year by only ~£14m, which sets the practical width. The mechanical projection was discounted not for tone but because its scale error is larger than the entire quantity being forecast.

Pre-exceptional basic EPS

No lens has guidance here — every estimate is an inference from the guided operating profit down to the bottom line, and that descent is where the money is. I weighted lens_margins and lens_forensics most, because they are the only views that carried the H1 arithmetic through rather than assuming flat conversion: H1 FY26 pre-exceptional PBT of £13.4m versus £19.0m, against H1 FY25 pre-exceptional EPS of 0.81p, implies H1 FY26 near 0.57-0.58p. Reaching FY25's 1.31p therefore requires an H2 that is materially stronger than H2 FY25 — possible on seasonality plus the c.£50m cost saves, but unguided. I was most tempted by the cluster at 1.25-1.30 (guidance, drivers, market, macro), which reads straight off flat operating profit; I set it aside because flat operating profit with a swing from net cash to intra-year net debt and Hays' historically high effective tax rate leaves EPS geared and asymmetric to the downside — at this profit level a £3-4m move in finance cost or tax charge is a fifth of the EPS. lens_guidance's stray reference to H1 FY26 pre-exceptional EPS of 0.02p (and lens_mechanical's 0.023 projection, which is the same figure rolled forward) is almost certainly a post-exceptional or mis-scaled read, but I cannot fully exclude it, so the p10 sits well below the analytic floor.

weighting: Materiality: with net income of only c.£20m on c.1.6bn shares, every 0.1p of EPS is c.£1.6m of post-tax profit — so tax rate and finance cost, which no lens has evidence on, dominate the answer more than the guided operating profit does. The 325% reproduction error on this series and the unresolved 0.02p/0.58p H1 conflict justify the widest band of the three metrics.

Pre-exceptional operating profit

Weighted decisively on lens_guidance and lens_margins, which both rest on Hays explicitly stating that FY26 pre-exceptional operating profit is expected to be in line with market consensus of £45.2m — a company-sourced forward statement made late in the year, essentially flat versus FY25's £45.6m, with the mechanism named (c.£50m annualised structural savings secured in FY26, c.£95m cumulative since FY24, offsetting continued fee erosion). A late-year confirmation of consensus by the company is about the tightest signal available for a full-year P&L line, and it is corroborated by the fee arithmetic: ~£898m of fees at a slightly improved conversion is consistent with £45m. lens_mechanical's £59.5m is the view I was most tempted to give some weight to, since it is the only genuinely independent read; I set it aside because lens_forensics showed its input series had the weak H1 divisional profit figures dropped as order-of-magnitude outliers, so it is extrapolating a pre-downturn trend the company has already contradicted. Downside skew reflects that 'in line with consensus' guidance issued before the year is closed can still slip on a soft final period, and that no peer or independent demand lens was available to test the H2 recovery embedded in it.

weighting: Materiality: this is the one metric where a company statement of the specific number exists, and one sigma of the series (£14.5m) is a third of the level — so anchoring on the guided figure rather than the trend extrapolation is worth roughly £14m of accuracy. Band width is set by what a late-year 'in line' statement can still miss, not by the spread of lens opinions, which is zero.

Absent views were named to it, not hidden: Two lenses abstained honestly and both would have covered the same gap: independent, non-Hays evidence on end-market conditions. lens_demand would have tested employer hiring budgets and candidate supply in Germany, UK&I and ANZ against Hays' own claim that declines are moderating (Q4 -5% versus Q2 -10%); lens_peer_read would have checked that moderation against PageGroup, Robert Walters, Randstad or Adecco reporting overlapping quarters. Without either, every fee and profit estimate here is ultimately circular on Hays' own commentary, and the H2 profit recovery implied by flat full-year operating profit against a 29% H1 PBT decline is untested by any outside source. That gap is why I skewed the operating profit and EPS distributions to the downside and kept the EPS band very wide, rather than treating the tight lens agreement as confirmation.

What the judge did.
Worldwide net sales and revenues (USDm)

I weighted lens_margins most heavily, because it is the only view that interrogated the definition of the number rather than the level of it. Its observation is decisive: the $10,731.5m figure that lens_mechanical, lens_forensics and lens_macro all land on is numerically identical to the sell-side consensus mean, and that consensus carries a stated year-ago comparator of $10,357m — which is Deere's equipment-operations net sales for Q3 FY25, not the $12,018m worldwide net sales and revenues total that this metric labels. Three lenses converging on that number is one signal restated three times (two of them explicitly say they are echoing the income model, and the model itself has evidently converged on consensus), and it is a signal about a different line item. Against that, the consistency argument is strong: Q1 FY26 +13% YoY, Q2 FY26 +4.7% YoY, and the Q2->Q3 sequential ratio of 0.86-0.94 across FY23-FY25 applied to $13,369m gives $11.5-12.6B; the YoY path off $12,018m gives $12.3-12.6B. Both roads run through $12.3B. The view I was most tempted by and set aside was lens_forensics, which flagged the discontinuity honestly rather than smoothing it, but then still anchored on the suspect figure instead of concluding the mismatch was definitional. I keep a fat left tail to $10.8B precisely because if I am wrong about the definition, the miss is roughly a full standard deviation of the series — the swing here is $3,970m, so getting the concept right dominates every other consideration in this metric.

weighting: Materiality of the definitional question. One standard deviation of this series is $3,970m; the gap between the two candidate answers is ~$1,600m, or 0.4 sigma, and it is entirely explained by whether the target is equipment net sales or total net sales and revenues. No refinement of growth-rate judgement is worth anything next to resolving that, so weight went to the single lens that resolved it rather than to the three that carried the ambiguity forward.

Diluted EPS (GAAP) (USD / share)

Seven views, coefficient of variation 0.0, every one of them at $4.70 — and that unanimity is worth less than it looks, because all seven are the same two arithmetic operations. Either take FY26 guidance midpoint $4.75B, subtract H1 actual $2.429B, split the $2.321B residual 55/45 using FY25's Q3/Q4 shape, divide by 270.7m shares; or take the Q3/Q2 seasonal ratio of 0.70-0.74 and apply it to $6.55. Both land at $4.70, and so does consensus. What none of them price is that the guidance-midpoint step assumes Deere lands mid-range, and that the seasonal step is calibrated on the same consensus that Deere has beaten repeatedly (Q2 FY25 $6.64 vs ~$5.61, Q3 FY25 $4.75 vs ~$4.35). lens_guidance was the most useful view here and it says so itself: with only one guidance data point in evidence it cannot estimate a landing-position bias, so it defaults to the midpoint. That is an honest statement that the central estimate is unbiased only by construction, not by measurement. I therefore shift the median modestly above the consensus cluster to $4.90 and skew the upper tail: at the $5.0B top of guided FY net income, H2 is $2.57B and a 55% Q3 share implies ~$5.22, so the upper half of my band is inside guidance rather than outside it. Most tempted by lens_margins, which reached $4.70 via two genuinely separate routes (sequential ratio and a mild-YoY-decline read) — but both routes inherit the same seasonal shape from the same two prior years, so they are less independent than presented. Swing on this metric is $5.95, which is enormous relative to the level, and the absence of any demand or peer read means I have no external check on H2 margin trajectory at all; hence a band nearly $1.40 wide.

weighting: Materiality of the unpriced asymmetry. One sigma of history is $5.95/share, so the entire seven-lens agreement occupies a sliver of the plausible range. Weight went to the guidance arithmetic because it is the only thing anchoring the level to a company statement, and then to the recognition — made explicitly by lens_guidance — that the midpoint assumption is unmeasured, which is worth more than six restatements of the same seasonal ratio.

Production & Precision Ag operating profit (USDm)

Six views spanning $494-565m, and the honest reading is that all of them are triangulating around a hole: no lens has a reported Q3 FY25 P&PA figure to anchor a YoY comparison, so every estimate runs through the FY24 Q2->Q3 ratio of 0.704 applied to the $706m Q2 FY26 base (~$497m) or the model's shrunk-growth extrapolation (~$563m). lens_margins did the most careful work — it built the estimate two ways, including reconstructing an implied Q3 FY25 of ~$808m and applying the observed -39% YoY compression, reaching ~$493m. I set that aside as the median only because I distrust the input series more than it does. lens_forensics raises the point that matters most: the model explicitly discarded the reported Q1 FY26 segment figures ($139m profit on $3,163m sales) as scale anomalies, so the trend line being extrapolated is not clean. There is also an unreconciled inconsistency in the evidence — P&PA net sales -14% YoY in Q2 FY26 while consolidated revenue was +4.7% YoY — which means either the segment is deteriorating far faster than the whole, or one of these figures is being read against a mismatched base. I cannot tell which, so I center at $535m, between the seasonal reconstruction and the model trend, and widen aggressively in both directions. Three lenses abstained here (demand, peer, guidance) and each abstention removes exactly the check that would resolve this: farm income and dealer inventory data, a CNH/AGCO large-ag read, and any segment-level outlook. That is not agreement, it is three separate statements that the segment's driver is unobservable in this corpus, and the band reflects it.

weighting: Materiality relative to a contaminated base series. One sigma is $267m against a $535m median — half the level — so the segment is intrinsically volatile before any evidence problem. The weight went to the two views that named a specific defect in the inputs (discarded Q1 anomaly, missing Q3 FY25 comparable) rather than to the tighter point estimates, because the size of the plausible error in the series exceeds the entire $70m spread between the surviving views.

Absent views were named to it, not hidden: No lens was formally absent, but three of nine abstained on two or all three metrics, and the abstentions cluster on exactly the questions that would discipline these numbers. lens_demand would have supplied the end-market read — USDA net farm income, corn and soybean prices, dealer new-equipment inventory and order backlogs — which is the single largest determinant of both consolidated revenue and P&PA margin; without it, every revenue and segment estimate here is a seasonal extrapolation of Deere's own prior prints with no external validation of whether the ag cycle is turning. lens_peer_read would have brought CNH, AGCO or Caterpillar disclosures covering roughly May-July 2026, which is the only way to separate market contraction from Deere-specific share or pricing movement; its absence is why I cannot narrow the P&PA band. lens_guidance abstained on revenue and on the segment because Deere gives only a consolidated full-year net income range, with no quarterly split and no history of guided-versus-actual landing positions in evidence — which means even the EPS estimate, the one metric anchored to a company statement, rests on an unmeasured assumption that Deere lands at the midpoint. I widened all three intervals rather than treating these silences as corroboration, most sharply on P&PA where all three gaps overlap, and I skewed the EPS upper tail because the missing landing-position history is the specific thing that would tell me whether the midpoint assumption is conservative.
